blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and the instruction, and samples SE(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA's intended motion chooses and reshapes the trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA's denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object's poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA's weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen π0.5 from 24.5% to 95.1%, above that of a π0.5 fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it steers. On a real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID π0.5 around an obstacle and to a placement at the limit of the arm's reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.

home. Vision-language-action models

Fine-tuning a VLA can teach it those layouts, but it needs robot demonstrations of every new scene and can make it
forget skills it already has [ 95 ] . Guidance instead changes what a generative model produces without
changing the model: each denoising step is nudged along the gradient of an objective. It has spread from image generation [ 15 ] to inverse
problems [ 13 , 66 ] , trajectory planning [ 35 ] and robot
policies [ 75 , 17 , 51 ] . Since current VLAs generate actions with flow-matching
experts [ 4 , 3 , 59 ] , the same recipe applies to them with no robot
data or training: OmniGuide [ 67 ] steers frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T by back-propagating 3D energies
through the robot’s kinematics. Its targets are local: a collision field does not know the goal, an attractor
pulls straight through obstacles and can get stuck in local minima, and both act on the gripper, not the object it
holds. The open question is not how to steer a frozen VLA, but where to.

blocks.en:
A route that helps a frozen VLA must meet several requirements, and existing planners each meet only some of them. It
must be metric and three-dimensional, unlike image paths, which lack
depth [ 25 , 45 ] . It must describe the held object and how it turns, not only the gripper
positions of 3D path predictors [ 34 , 33 ] . Models of 6-DoF object
motion [ 84 , 87 , 64 ] plan the object, but learn from human data, without
its shape or the robot’s reach. It must cover the whole carry and find the goal from the instruction, whereas motion
planners [ 40 , 70 ] must be given the goal. It must reach the VLA without
retraining it, whereas hierarchical VLAs [ 45 , 34 , 7 ] train their low-level
policy to follow plans. Above all, the route and the VLA must agree. Together they form a hierarchy, a planner of the route above a planner
of actions, and in hierarchies the high level usually commands while the low level is trained to obey. A frozen VLA has its
own preferred motion, and a route chosen without it has to be forced on it. A high level that offers a distribution of
routes can instead couple with the VLA at test time, with feedback in both directions: the VLA’s intended motion chooses and reshapes the route, and the
route steers the VLA.

blocks.en:
We present Cairn, a framework that steers frozen VLAs with 3D trajectories of the held object that account for the
scene, its obstacles and the object’s own shape. The name comes from the stacked stones that mark a hiking trail: a
cairn shows the way but carries no one along it. In the same way, Cairn marks the route of the held object and
leaves the moving to the VLA. To meet the requirements above, it builds a two-level planner from a small 3D
specialist, which plans the route, and the frozen 2D generalist, which plans the actions ( Fig. 2 ). The specialist is a motion prior built like 3D point-cloud
policies [ 23 , 24 ] , but it predicts where the held object travels rather than
how the robot moves. From point clouds of the scene and the
held object, along with its pose at the grasp and the instruction, it samples with rectified
flow [ 52 ] a route to the release as SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) waypoints. It is trained without robot actions, on
simulated demonstrations generated with moved objects, obstacles and several routes per scene. At test time the prior and the VLA
steer each other. The VLA’s intended motion weights and refines the sampled routes that clear the scene. In turn, at
every denoising step, the object motion that the VLA’s action chunk would produce is pulled toward the next waypoint of
the chosen route. The VLA’s weights are never changed.

We evaluate Cairn in simulation and on a real robot. On LIBERO-Shift, 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with moved objects
and obstacles, it raises the success of the frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} from 24.5% to 95.1%, more than fine-tuning π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on the same layouts, which also degrades π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on standard LIBERO, where Cairn leaves performance
unchanged. On LIBERO-PRO [ 93 ] , a third-party benchmark of moved objects, it raises π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s
success on the episodes it steers from 54.4% to 81.1%.
The coupling between the two levels helps where success has room: under LIBERO-PRO’s layout shift it adds
2.3 points over a route fixed at the grasp, and where the VLA’s intent changes the route it makes motion
smoother and safer. On a real Franka, with a
prior trained only in simulation, Cairn steers the frozen DROID π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} around an obstacle and to a
placement at the limit of the arm’s reach, where π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} alone fails. Our contributions are: • Cairn, to our knowledge the first framework that steers a frozen VLA with learned SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) routes of the object it
holds, from grasp to release, conditioned on the scene, the object’s shape and the instruction. • A hierarchical planner whose two levels, a learned route prior and a frozen VLA, inform each other at test time
in both directions, without retraining either. • A generator of varied LIBERO demonstrations, with moved objects, obstacles that force detours and turns, and
several routes per scene, and LIBERO-Shift, a held-out benchmark built with it. • Extensive experiments in simulation and on a real robot showing that Cairn makes frozen VLAs robust to moved
objects and obstacles, outperforms fine-tuning without its forgetting, and carries over to a third-party

blocks.en: 2 Related work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
VLAs adapt pre-trained vision-language models to map images and an instruction to robot actions [ 6 , 39 , 4 , 3 , 59 ] . The π \pi family
generates action chunks with a flow-matching expert [ 4 , 3 ] . Near-saturated
LIBERO scores [ 48 ] hide a reliance on the training layouts: moving objects or changing initial states
collapses success [ 93 , 20 , 73 , 19 ] . Fine-tuning on more
varied data, e.g . generated procedurally [ 56 , 22 , 80 ] , needs
robot actions for every new layout and can cause forgetting [ 95 ] . Hierarchical VLAs train a
low-level policy to follow a 2D or 3D end-effector path [ 25 , 45 , 42 , 34 , 33 , 49 ] or a latent plan [ 59 , 90 , 7 , 10 ] from a high-level model. The planner can learn from
non-robot data, but the coupling is fixed in training and relearned for every embodiment, executors may ignore the plan [ 77 ] , and the plan gives the gripper’s position, not the held object’s pose. Feedback runs only from the plan down, whereas
hierarchical planners also revise the high level with low-level outcomes: route progress [ 62 ] ,
predicted control costs [ 57 ] , or low-level proposals during joint diffusion
sampling [ 28 ] . DreamTrajectory [ 82 ] fine-tunes π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} to predict a short end-effector trajectory and keeps the chunks
that realise it, so it cannot add scene geometry the policy lacks. We instead couple a frozen generalist VLA at test
time, in both directions, with a learned prior over the held object’s SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) route, trained without robot actions.

blocks.en:
Diffusion and flow samplers can be biased without retraining by guidance [ 15 ] and its variants on
the clean-sample estimate [ 13 , 66 , 83 , 21 ] , inpainting [ 55 ] or products of models [ 29 , 50 , 18 ] . Most methods that
steer robot policies add the gradient of an energy to the denoising update and differ in where the target comes from:
human goal points and sketches [ 75 ] , goal images scored by a learned dynamics model [ 17 ] , VLM-selected keyframes [ 27 ] or VLM-written stage rewards [ 51 ] , a
learned critic [ 81 ] , collision costs [ 44 , 26 ] , or, to hide latency, the previous
action chunk [ 5 ] . Gradient-free methods rank sampled actions with a value function or a verifier [ 58 , 65 , 41 , 53 , 14 , 46 ] , act on the
initial noise [ 72 ] , or compose policies [ 8 ] .
Pretrained generative models have also been coupled at test time, by soft terms on their clean estimates [ 1 ] , coupling costs [ 54 ] , guidance through a shared embedding [ 78 ] or a known measurement [ 12 , 43 ] , Gibbs sampling over
projections of a shared state [ 74 ] , or joint sampling of a planner with a model-based
optimiser [ 36 ] . OmniGuide [ 67 ] back-propagates 3D energies
through differentiable kinematics into the denoising of frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T: a collision repeller, an attractor at
a VLM-pointed target, and end-effector waypoints from a human video or a motion plan. Its authors note that such fields
cannot reliably avoid local minima. Like OmniGuide, we steer through the robot’s kinematics, but toward a global route
of the held object, including its rotation, from a learned prior that is itself steered by the VLA’s intent, with no
VLM or human video at test time.

blocks.en:
3D policies [ 23 , 37 , 24 , 86 ] predict actions from
calibrated point clouds; they are sample-efficient and precise but trained per benchmark. Our planner adopts their architecture to predict the held object’s route instead of actions. Object-centric
methods turn predicted object motion into robot motion: point flow [ 85 , 2 , 79 , 91 ] , SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) object poses from
demonstrations [ 30 ] or generated videos [ 61 , 89 ] mapped to the gripper by
a rigid grasp, or poses that condition a trained action head [ 68 ] . Models of 6-DoF object motion, learned
from human egocentric and hand-object data, generate a trajectory from language and the scene [ 84 , 16 , 87 ] or complete an observed one toward a given goal pose [ 64 , 88 ] . They describe the held object by its pose, category or bounding box rather than
its shape, avoid collisions at most with its centre [ 64 ] , do not check that a robot can execute the
motion, and when executed are retargeted open loop in place of the controller [ 87 ] . Motion planners
compute collision-free robot paths to a given goal by sampling or optimisation [ 40 , 70 ] or from learned diffusion priors [ 35 , 9 , 11 ] . VLMs can supply the goal as value maps, keypoint
constraints or 3D traces [ 31 , 32 , 92 ] for a planner to execute. Our prior
learns from robot-executed routes, sees the held object’s shape, infers the goal from language, and steers a policy
rather than replacing it.

We consider rigid pick-and-place: given an instruction, the robot grasps an object and carries it to a placement.
The frozen VLA stays the controller; what it lacks in a new layout is where the object should go. A
learned motion prior proposes routes of the held object ( Sec. 3.1 ). It is trained on
generated demonstrations ( Sec. 3.2 ), and at test time the prior and the VLA steer each other
( Sec. 3.3 , Fig. 2 ).

The prior builds on 3DFA [ 24 ] but reads 3D geometry directly and gives the held object a
branch of its own. The object’s cloud is removed from the scene and encoded separately by a point MLP, posed at the
grasp, so the prior sees the shape of what it carries. The scene is encoded from its cloud by a Point Transformer
V3 [ 76 ] , where 3DFA lifts features from camera images. Scene and object tokens attend to each other and
to CLIP features of the instruction [ 63 ] , and keep their 3D positions for spatial attention. The start
pose enters as a token that embeds A A itself, where 3DFA uses a learned query. At flow time, it modulates
3DFA’s flow head in place of the gripper’s state. The encoder runs once per input and is reused at every sampling step.

blocks.en:
The prior can learn goal-following, obstacle-aware routes only if its data contains them.
LIBERO’s [ 48 ] do not: the roughly 50 human demonstrations of a task share one layout and no obstacles,
and their routes differ by only 2–4 cm on average, so they teach one route per task.

LIBERO的[48]没有:大约50个人类的一次任务展示有一个布局,没有障碍,
他们的路线平均只有2–4厘米,所以他们每个任务教一条路线。

blocks.en:
We therefore generate demonstrations that vary these factors ( Fig. 3 ). As in
MimicGen [ 56 , 22 ] , each demonstration re-anchors a human one to a new
layout: the grasp follows the object, the placement is solved for the new receptacle, and the human carry is stretched
between them. The receptacle is moved, and the start and clutter are re-sampled, so the goal must come from the scene
and the instruction (iii). Obstacles from six families are placed on the nominal path, and each layout is generated
without and with them. For gate, pole and bar, a long object passes only by turning (i, ii). Each scene also receives
alternative routes left of, right of or over each obstacle, or bowing in open scenes (iv).

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion and future work
blocks.zh: 5. 结论和今后的工作

blocks.en:
We presented Cairn, which steers a frozen VLA with a learned prior over the 3D route of the object in its gripper.
The prior and the VLA form the two levels of one planner. The prior proposes SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) routes from the scene, the held
object and the instruction, and the VLA’s intent selects and refines them. The chosen route then pulls the VLA’s
denoising toward its next waypoint, while the VLA still grasps and sets its own pace. Because the route belongs
to the object, the prior needs no robot actions and turns long objects through gaps, and it transfers from simulation
to a real robot. Because the VLA is never retrained, it keeps its skills. In the future, the prior could also learn from
videos of people moving objects, toward a foundation model of object motion paired with generalist VLAs.

对一个真正的机器人。 因为VLA从未再被再训练过,所以保留了自己的技能. 今后,先辈还可以学习
